title: The Embodiment of Architectural Experience: A Methodological Perspective on Neuro-Architecture
research_question: To examine the current state of neuro-architecture, identify methodological limitations, and propose a path for advancing the understanding of cognitive processes underlying human architectural experience and inspiring evidence-based architectural design principles, particularly by integrating ecological psychology and mobile brain/body imaging.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Static visual stimuli of architectural environments, including 2D images of architectural designs.
Images of curvilinear architectural interiors vs. rectilinear interiors.
Virtual rooms with higher ceilings vs. enclosed rooms.
Images of buildings labeled as sourced from a gallery vs. computer-generated.
Window shapes in building facades (rectangular, square, circular, semi-circular arches vs. triangle, triangular arches).
Virtual architectural spaces with manipulated geometrical aspects (scale, proportion, protrusion, curvature).
Restorative environments (e.g., buildings with vegetation-surrounding) vs. low restorative potential environments.
Enclosed virtual room without windows vs. virtual room with windows.
Virtual architectural spaces with three kinds of door transitions differing in passability (narrow, medium, wide doors).

findings.mechanism: Hippocampal contribution to processing architectural ranking.
findings.quote: buildings that rank high regarding their social status as they are designed to be more important (like government buildings) or sublime (like religious buildings) have more impact on the perception of sublimity
participants perceived curvilinear spaces as more beautiful than rectilinear ones

findings.antecedent: Curvilinear architectural interiors (when making approach-avoidance decisions)
findings.consequent: Activation of lingual and calcarine gyrus in visual cortex
findings.quote: images of curvilinear architectural interiors activated the lingual and the calcarine gyrus in the visual cortex more than images of rectilinear interiors
curvilinear contours activated the anterior cingulate cortex exclusively
rooms with higher ceilings were more likely to be judged as beautiful

findings.consequent: Activation of structures involved in visuospatial exploration and attention in the dorsal stream
findings.quote: activated structures involved in visuospatial exploration and attention in the dorsal stream
Open rooms were judged as more beautiful compared with enclosed rooms

findings.consequent: Activation of regions in the temporal lobes associated with perceived visual motion
findings.quote: activated regions in the temporal lobes associated with perceived visual motion

findings.antecedent: Image labeled as sourced from a gallery (vs. computer generated)
findings.mechanism: Expectations about aesthetic value moderate aesthetic judgment.
findings.quote: if the same image was labeled as being sourced from a gallery rather than being computer generated, its aesthetic ratings were significantly higher

findings.antecedent: Image labeled as sourced from a gallery (vs. computer generated)
findings.consequent: Neural activity in medial orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and prefrontal cortex (PFC)
findings.mechanism: Neural mechanisms involved in aesthetic ratings difference.
findings.quote: The neural mechanisms involved in this difference in aesthetic ratings were traced to the medial orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and the prefrontal cortex (PFC)

findings.antecedent: Architects (vs. non-architects) making aesthetic judgments about buildings
findings.consequent: Activity in bilateral medial OFC and subcallosal cingulate gyrus
findings.mechanism: Expertise modulates response in reward-related brain areas.
findings.quote: architects, compared with non-architects, had increased activity of the bilateral medial OFC and the subcallosal cingulate gyrus, when making aesthetic judgments about buildings

findings.antecedent: Pleasant window shapes (rectangular, square, circular, semi-circular arches)
findings.quote: rectangular, square, circular and semi-circular arches were considered as pleasant window shapes
windows with triangle and triangular arches were determined as unpleasant

findings.consequent: ERP effect in the left hemisphere
findings.mechanism: Consistent with notions of lateralization with regards to emotional processes.
findings.quote: the effect of pleasant stimuli was larger in the left hemisphere than that of unpleasant ones
large symmetrical spaces positively affect users

findings.antecedent: Extreme change of proportion in height P(H) or width P(W) of virtual spaces
findings.quote: the more extreme a change of proportion in height P(H) or width P(W) of virtual spaces was displayed, the stronger the response of distress was observed

findings.antecedent: Manipulations in geometry of virtual space
findings.quote: All physiological measurements demonstrated significantly increased signals in non-designers than those of designers

findings.antecedent: Exposure to restorative environments (e.g., buildings with vegetation-surrounding)
findings.consequent: Activation of middle frontal gyrus, middle and inferior temporal gyrus, insula, inferior parietal lobe, and cuneus
findings.quote: exposure to restorative environments (like buildings with vegetation-surrounding) led to activation of the middle frontal gyrus, middle and inferior temporal gyrus, insula, inferior parietal lobe, and cuneus
endogenous, top-down, directed attention is more active during viewing of low restorative potential vs. high restorative potential environments
participants immersed in an enclosed virtual room without windows exhibited greater reactivity to a stress test than those in a virtual room with windows

findings.antecedent: Stress state (induced by enclosed virtual room without windows)
findings.quote: Physiological reactions of this stress state consisted of both heightened and prolonged spikes in salivary cortisol

findings.antecedent: Curvature geometries of interior forms (during active exploration)
findings.consequent: Brain activity in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC)
findings.quote: curvature geometries of interior forms influenced brain activity originating from the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC)

findings.consequent: Brain activity in posterior cingulate cortex and occipital lobe
findings.quote: the posterior cingulate cortex and the occipital lobe were involved in the processing of different room perspectives

findings.antecedent: Different transition affordances (door widths: narrow, medium, wide)
findings.quote: Different transition affordances influenced the architectural experience of participants. Different door widths influenced participants' emotional experience, especially when instructed to pass through the door

findings.consequent: Brain activity in visual sensory regions and motor areas (around 200 ms)
findings.mechanism: Automated processing of the affordance, irrespective of planned interaction.
findings.quote: brain activity in visual sensory regions and motor areas reflected the affordance of the transition already around 200 ms, irrespective of whether participants knew that they should or should not pass into the second room

findings.consequent: Additional affordance-specific modulations of brain activity (PINV)
findings.quote: differences in the post-imperative negative variation (PINV)... were visible only in trials that required an interaction with the environment (Go-trials) while in the NoGo condition, this architectural affordance effect was not observed

findings.mechanism: Information is embedded in imminent action and perceived during exploration, not via signal transformation/representation/computation.
findings.quote: possibilities of imminent actions shape our perception

mechanisms: Neural basis of human perception of and interaction with the surrounding architecture.
Cognitive processes underlying human experience in built environments.
Expectations about aesthetic value moderating aesthetic judgment.
Expertise modulating reward-related brain responses to architecture.
Lateralization of emotional processes in the brain.
Endogenous, top-down, directed attention in low restorative potential environments.
Embodied exploration in architectural experience as a perception-action loop.
Automated processing of affordances in the built environment.
Information embedded in imminent action and perceived during exploration.
implementation_implications: Neuroscience can improve the design process, design strategies, and inform regulations to improve human health and well-being.
Building-integrated vegetation can be considered for architects to improve stress-restoration for residents.
Architectural affordances can be used to alter the behavior of users.
New insights from MoBI can be used to improve architectural design strategies and regulations to eventually improve human health and well-being.
limitations: The majority of existing neuro-architectural studies are confined to architectural aesthetics, not regarding other aspects of architecture like ergonomics, affordances, or functionality.
Existing neuro-architectural research often restricts participants to remain stationary, preventing naturalistic interaction with architectural surroundings.
The low ecological validity of established brain imaging methods (e.g., fMRI, stationary EEG) due to restrictions on participant mobility.
Data collection in stationary participants experiencing 2D images of architectural designs results in reduced ecological validity.
The interaction with the environment can become relatively complex in terms of sensory information and motor behavior, requiring cautious and systematic approaches in MoBI studies.

paper_metadata.title: The Embodiment of Architectural Experience: A Methodological Perspective on Neuro-Architecture
paper_metadata.crossref_title: The Embodiment of Architectural Experience: A Methodological Perspective on Neuro-Architecture
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: People spend a large portion of their time inside built environments. Research in neuro-architecture—the neural basis of human perception of and interaction with the surrounding architecture—promises to advance our understanding of the cognitive processes underlying this common human experience and also to inspire evidence-based architectural design principles. This article examines the current state of the field and offers a path for moving closer to fulfilling this promise. The paper is structured in three sections, beginning with an introduction to neuro-architecture, outlining its main objectives and giving an overview of experimental research in the field. Afterward, two methodological limitations attending current brain-imaging architectural research are discussed: the first concerns the limited focus of the research, which is often restricted to the aesthetic dimension of architectural experience; the second concerns practical limitations imposed by the typical experimental tools and methods, which often require participants to remain stationary and prevent naturalistic interaction with architectural surroundings. Next, we propose that the theoretical basis of ecological psychology provides a framework for addressing these limitations and motivates emphasizing the role of embodied exploration in architectural experience, which encompasses but is not limited to aesthetic contemplation. In this section, some basic concepts within ecological psychology and their convergences with architecture are described. Lastly, we introduce Mobile Brain/Body Imaging (MoBI) as one emerging brain imaging approach with the potential to improve the ecological validity of neuro-architecture research. Accordingly, we suggest that combining theoretical and conceptual resources from ecological psychology with state-of-the-art neuroscience methods (Mobile Brain/Body Imaging) is a promising way to bring neuro-architecture closer to accomplishing its scientific and practical goals.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Architectural experience is fundamentally shaped by the body's interaction with and perception of the environment, integrating sensory, motor, and affective processes.

The brain constantly generates predictions about the environment, and architectural experience arises from the interplay between these predictions and incoming sensory information, minimizing prediction errors.
Architectural environments offer 'affordances' – opportunities for action – that are directly perceived by individuals and influence their behavior and experience within a space.

mechanism_chain.description: A proposed theoretical mechanism for how architectural features influence human experience, integrating embodied and neural perspectives.

steps.from_construct: Architectural spatial properties (e.g., ceiling height, openness, material textures)
steps.to_construct: Embodied perception of space (e.g., perceived spaciousness, sense of enclosure, haptic feedback)
Neural activation patterns (e.g., in sensorimotor, limbic, and default mode networks)
Affective states (e.g., awe, comfort, stress) and Cognitive processes (e.g., attention, memory, creativity)

instruments_used.name: fMRI
instruments_used.construct: Brain activity related to spatial cognition, emotion, and aesthetic processing in architectural contexts
instruments_used.description: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging to measure changes in blood flow associated with neural activity.

instruments_used.name: EEG
instruments_used.construct: Temporal dynamics of brain electrical activity during architectural perception and interaction
instruments_used.description: Electroencephalography to measure electrical activity in the brain via electrodes placed on the scalp.

instruments_used.name: Eye-tracking
instruments_used.construct: Visual attention, gaze patterns, and exploration strategies within architectural environments
instruments_used.description: Device to record eye movements and fixations.

instruments_used.name: Electrodermal Activity (EDA)
instruments_used.construct: Physiological arousal and emotional responses to architectural stimuli
instruments_used.description: Measurement of changes in electrical conductance of the skin, often referred to as Galvanic Skin Response (GSR).

instruments_used.name: Heart Rate Variability (HRV)
instruments_used.construct: Autonomic nervous system activity, stress, and relaxation in response to architectural environments
instruments_used.description: Measurement of the variation in the time interval between consecutive heartbeats.
